ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Proposal for Human Genome Sequencing by CCMB, Hyderabad 
*181. SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that former direct or of Centre of Cellular and Molecular 
Biology, Hyderabad, had submitted to the De partment of Biotechnology, in 1989, the 
human genome sequencing project by our scientists; 
(b) whether it is a also a fact that the Department has confined the proposal to the 
cold storage; and 
(c) if so, the reasons for not approving the proposal in 1989? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI) (a) In April 1989, a letter was received by the Government from 
the former Director of Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad 
regarding the Human Genome Sequencing Pr ogramme by national scientists. This 
also indicated a tentative cost of Rs. 300 crores for 15 years; 
(b) and (c) No, Sir. The Department of Biotechnology with large number of 
experts from the country, analysed the position. It was decided that it would be 
worthwhile to take up an Indian progra mme on genome sequencing that is more 
relevant to country's specific needs and would be economically feasible. The Expert 
Committee accordingly recommended to init iate development technologies for 
identifying known mutations in specific genetic disorders in the Indian 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [ 4 August, 2000] 
population and initiating studies on human genome diversity. Programmes presently 
are under implementation in these area s and the country is well poised in 
infrastructure and trained human resource to  take on the work in functional genomics, 
one of the most important component of the human genomics and related areas. 
SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY: Mr. Chairman, Sir,  the hon. Minister's written reply is 
not very comprehensive. The recent announcement of the virtual completion of the 
human genome sequency pr oject is widely regarded as one of the most important 
advances in the history of science. In 1988, when the U.S. had decided to invest in this 
project, which subsequently became an intern ational project, with the participation of 
even countries such as China and Japan, but not India, the then Director of the Centre 
for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad, Dr. Bhargava, wrote a letter to the 
then Prime Minister, Shri Rajiv Gandhi, sugges ting that India should also invest in the 
human genome project. He has stated that India could do it at a much lower cost than 
the U.S., that is, in Rs. 300 crores, whic h would mean Rs. 200 crores per annum. As 
usual, the Prime Minister's Office refe rred his letter to the Department of 
Biotechnology, who have shelved it on flimsy grounds. Even though Dr. Bhargava 
played a vital role in the setting up of the Biotechnology Department and was a 
member of its high powered Scientific Advisory Committee for many years, why did 
not the Department of the Biotechnology acknowledge his letter? Why did not the 
Biotechnology Department communicate the reasons for it being shelved? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, in order to keep the record straight, let me 
trace the history of this whole episode. The hon. Member has referred to his great 
project about which a recent announcement ha s been made by the US President and 
the UK Prime Minister about the advances in human genome research and the number 
of diseases and hereditary defects whic h could cured as a result of scientific 
investigations in this fiel d. It has been pointed out the a letter was written by the 
former Director to the then Prime Minister. Let me say that this letter which the hon. 
Member has referred to was written by Prof. Bhargava to the then Prime Minister of 
India sometime in April, 1989. This letter was not written to the 
6 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Department of Biotechnology . It was addressed to the Prime Minister. The Prime 
Minister's Office did not send any referenc e to the Department of Biotechnology till 
19th February, 1990, and that was also, perh aps, as a result of a letter from Prof. 
Bhargava to the then Minister of Scienc e and Technology, Prof. Menon, enclosing a 
copy of his earlier letter, along with Prof. Menon's letter. In that he had specifically 
mentioned to prevent a meeting of the scientists in the genetic field which was being 
held with Prof. Canter who was the Director of the Human Genome Centre at 
Lawrence Berkley Laboratory in USA. The fact of the case is like  this. In 1986, Dr. 
Watson in the USA announced this programme, and in 1988, this Human Genome 
Organisation was set up to coordinate international efforts. Now, at the 1986 meeting, 
the only scientist who was invited from India was Dr. Sharat Chandra; he was the only 
Indian and he is, perhaps, one of the finest  genetic researchers in this country. Prof. 
Bhargava was not invited to this meeting.  When Dr. Sharat Chandra came back, he 
discussed this project with the Secretary of Biotechnology Department. The Department 
was established only in 1986. Immediately, the Department starte d discussions with 
various scientists in the country and as a resu lt of that, they also tried to find out what 
projects can be undertaken in India and how  this project can benefit the people of 
India. As a result of this, a meeting was held on February 14th 1990. The USA also 
did not start the project in 1986 or 1988. The launched the project in 1990 and 
projected a cost of three billion dollars fo r 15 years. The Indian scientists assembled 
on 14th February, 1990. Prof. Cantor was invited to this. They discussed this and after 
that, they decided—the minutes say—that Indi a should not and cannot join that sort of 
a costly project. They decided that India should take India-specific projects as research 
project. Now we see we have four or five important activi ties going on under this 
project. So, there has been no shelving of th is project or putting it in cold storage. 
Indian scientists are very serious. They ha ve established 52 centres of bio-informatics 
and four genomic data centres where th ey are collecting the data. Ten thousand 
scientists are working in off-loading data  and using this data. They are studying 
genetic disorders, human genome diversit y projects, functional genomics. This is 
most important because what we want is this . We want that this research should lead 
to the direct 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
benefit to the common Indian masses. For example, Malaria is a very virulent disease. 
Now, we must discover vaccin es of Malaria. We want to do this research here. Prof. 
Bhargava had pointed out that we shoul d undertake this project for two reasons; 
firstly, it will be much cheaper in India, secondly, the data collected by the USA will 
not be available to Indians. On both c ounts, he was incorrect. The very first 
announcement and the recent announcement of President Clinton—I read out the 
extracts of the last few lines—says, "T he Human Genome Project, which completed 
its version of the working draft two years ahead of the schedule and under Budget, 
will continue its long standing practice of making all of its sequential data available to 
public and privately funded researchers world-wide, at non cost." So, his apprehension 
that this will not be available to Indians was ill founded. Even in earlier discussion, 
Dr. Watson had said that this data would be available in the public domain. 
The third point is about the cost. Number one: He had not mentioned about any 
Project. He had not given any detailed projec t report. He had only said that, perhaps, 
India could invest for 15 years a sum of Rs. 150—300 crores. May I most humbly 
inform the House that this was totally a gr oss underestimation of the cost. The cost, at 
that time was probably Rs. 80 lakhs per machine. Sir, America had put up some 300 
machines and, considering the size of human material available here, we have to put 
up about 1000 machines. So, there was no question of spending Rs. 150—300 crores. It 
would have been somewhere around Rs. 700— 800 crores for the machines alone. 
Then, chemicals and other usables are very costly. They have to be imported. The 
only component which is cheaper here is the salary of the scientists and such other 
costs. So, the Indian scientists fully deliberated. 
Another part of the issue was this. Dr. Bh argava was invited to attend the meeting 
on 14th February, 1990, but he refused to at tend the meeting. He was a Member of 
several Committees and, wherever the subject was discussed, he participated in some of 
them. But, I am surprised, after having dealt with all these questions by the researchers 
of this country, the great scientists of th is country, why this question is now being 
raised when the Indian Biotechnology a nd Genetic Research is moving forward and 
has done a very useful 
8 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
work? Therefore, the information given to  the hon. Member is incomplete and, I 
think, the record must be set right. There is no dereliction of duty on the part of the 
Department of Biotechnology. It  is fully taking cognisance of this Project. It is active 
on this Project and is making useful contribution towards this Project. 
SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY: The Minister has given a wrong reply. Anyway, we have 
missed the bus in regard to sequencing of the human genome. Dr. Bhargava suggested 
last year to the D.G. of the I.C.M.R. that a committee be constituted to analyse the 
sequences of the genomes of various organi sms. It was widely recognised even a few 
years ago that the major experiment in biology  in this century is going to the area of 
application of genome analysis in medical and health care, agriculture and sociology. 
Human genome sequence would also result in significant changes in our future life-
styles. 
The Committee was constituted and it has held  three meetings. But, surprisingly, 
the minutes of this meeting, with specific recommendations, were not circulated 
among the Members. May I know from the hon. Minister whether this Committee 
had submitted any proposal to the Secretary, Department of Biotechnology? If yes; 
why have they not been approved? I understand, the Secretary, Department of 
Biotechnology, had raised some frivolous objections in spite of the tremendous support 
from other Members. Does the hon. Minister know about it? If so, what measures the 
Minister would take to give clearance to this proposal? 
Finally, I suggest to the Minister th at analysis of genomes, including human 
genome, should be taken up as a major na tional mission under the Chairmanship of 
Dr. Abdul Kalam, with the I.C.M.R. as  the nodal agency and with financial 
contributions from other rela ted departments. As has been estimated, initially, the 
project would cost Rs. 50 crores, over a period of five years ...(Interruptions)... It is a 
technical question ...(Interruptions)... Please sit down ...(Interruptions)... I also 
suggest that the progress of the work on the project should be monitored by a high-
powered committee by involving some of the world's best known and socially committed 
scientists whose interests transcend national boundaries and who have been extremely 
sympathetic to India. Will the Minister 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
accept this suggestion and bring India on the map of human genome project? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI*. Sir, India is already on the map of international 
research. Some of our labs are doing very good work. For example, India has 3,496 
entries, as seen from the National Centre for Biotechnological Information, NIH, USA. 
Of this, sixty per cent of Indian origin, that is 2798 is from India. It means, India must 
have contributed at least 1500 kb. The contribution of labs which are working on it is, 
CCMB 59 kb, Indian Institute of Science 227  kb, South Campus of Delhi University 
67 kb, JNU 296 kb, and NH 65 kb. So, you win that all of them are active. Some of 
our vaccines, some of our work, which has been done by our scientists, have been 
widely recognised. I need not go into those details. So far as this Committee which the 
ICMR has decided to constitute, or it is recommending, is concerned, we have not 
received any recommendations. Perhaps those recommendations are not final. Moreover, 
the ICMR is not under my Ministry. As and when they send a report, we shall consider 
it on merits. There is no proposal to th e Department of Biotechnology from anybody. 
Let me also make one point dear that I ha ve gone through the scientific work of this 
former Director, who is writing and saying so many things about genetics. Out of all this 
papers, I don't find even a tingle paper on genetics or on human genome. He is a 
biochemist. The only paper which I have seen , out of this list, does not deal with 
genetics. (Interruptions) 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, he is going out of the way. (Interruptions) 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: The question is, therefore, that recommendations 
or suggestions...(lnterruptions) 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: He is a very distinguished scientist. (Interruptions). He

DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: His name is being constantly referred to as one of

Therefore, we win examine ...{Interuptions)... The question is, whenever there is a

DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is no doubt that the breakthrough 
in sequencing of human genome is a major development which has profound implications 
and implications for our life-style, for dis ease control, and ever for development of 
agriculture. It has been a collaborative effort in which, I believe, apart from the scientists

DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, the fa ct that China has done something in 
human genome research is ill-founded. The only two countries who have contributed 
mainly anything worthwhile are, USA and UK, and a small contribution is from France. 
Now we have a mission already working on genomics and one part is on rice genomics. 
On this part of human genomics now, as I have already indicated, we have 52 bio in formatic 
centres. There are four genomic centres fro m where we collect the data and 10,000 
scientists are working to offload this data round the clock. 
DR. RAJA RAMANNA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, India, unfortunately, has been- missing 
chances of being in the forefront of research at various stages of our history during the last 
50 yean. For instance, in hardware electronics, by taking wrong decisions, we have gone 
back. Instead of being in the forefront, we still depend on other countries from whom we 
are importing IC etc This question that has been 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [ 4 August, 2000] 
raised is of importance, in the sense—have  we missed another has with respect to the 
genomics project? The hon. Minister however has been good enough to tell us that the work 
is going on. Now, if it is a matter of purely technical value and technical importance, of 
the work that has been done then, it is a subject for discussion in the technical group and 
not be a part the hon. House here, because they would not have all the facts at their 
disposal. Especially, the quality of somebody's work and the papers that have been 
published, these are matters which should be judged by experts. I am somewhat sorry that the 
discussion has taken a turn in that direction. In any, case, I would recommend to this House 
that the genome project should be taken up with all the strength that we have, that is, 
with all the scientists working together in cohesion because it is a very difficult project but 
a very important one for the country. 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: I entirely agree with the former Minister that in many 
areas, during the past several years, we could not catch up with the rest of the world, and, 
in certain cases, we did miss the opportunity. There may still be some cases where we may 
not be going as fast as we should. But let me assure the House that in the field of 
biotechnology we are not missing any bus. Rather, our Department, within a very short 
period of 14 years—it was established only in 1986—it is now on the international map. 
Let me assure him that with 10,000 scientists working round the clock to offload data, to 
study the sequencing of the chromosomes and genes and trying to use them for discovering 
various peptides which would be useful fo r curing diseases, hereditary diseases, and 
genetic deformations. We are also in touch with some of the Indian drug companies to use 
this data and to come forward with certain cures and drugs for the benefit of the people 
in India. So, we are not missing the bus. But certainly, we cannot compete with a country 
like USA. We must also realise that we ha ve our own limitations and, within those 
limitations, I can assure this House that this Government will take alt necessary steps and 
will leave no stone unturned to put India on the international map in the field of genetic 
research. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) JOYASREE GOSWAMI MAHANTA: Sir, I appreciate the idea of 
the human genome sequencing project that has 
12

been presented by the Director, Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad. Sir, 
I would like to know whether the Government has thought of taking any immidiate steps 
which would be feasible, to enable the scientists and students to cany on with the work—
with the help of this idea of a project—w hich will be less costly and less time-
consuming. My second part Is: Is any such type of research going on in any university 
or research centre in our country with Government help? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, as I have already indi cated, there are 52 
centres from where we are collecting the data and we are conn ected with the rest of 
the world through satellites and other connectiv ities so that any data which is found 
anywhere in this field is available to us . We nave certain centres, very important 
centres, and they are working; students are working; universities are ate coating up and 
picking up. At I intimated to you, this is a subject which is of a very recent origin in 
India. Still, the JNU campus here, the South Campus and the Indian Institute of Science, all

Population Growth 
*184. SHRI RAJU PARMAR:  
SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted any study to find out the causes of failure 
of population control drive, despite plan ned programmes involvi ng huge expenditure 
both by the Central and State Governments, besides NGOs and individuals; 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof; and 
(c) what effective steps are contemplated to ensure perceptible control of 
population growth as the country enters the 21st Century? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
(a) and (b) The results of the Sample Registration System reveal that the Birth Rate, in 
the country had declined to 26.5 in 1998 fro m 40.8 in 1951; the total Fertility Rate, 
which was 6.0 in 1951 declined to 3.3 in  1997 and the natural growth rate of 
population has come down to 1.75% during the year 1998. This decline in birth rate 
has been observed despite death rate declining more sharply and life expectancy at 
birth increasing almost to double since independence due to improved health services 
in the country. 
Currently the population is growing rapidl y due to: (i) large size of the population 
in the reproductive age group (estimated cont ribution 60%); (ii) higher fertility due to 
unmet needs to contraception (estimated contribution 20%); and (iii) high wanted 
fertility due to prevailing hi gh infant mortality rate (estimated contribution about 
20%). 
(c) In order to speed up the efforts of population stabi lization in the country, 
Government has adopted the National Popul ation Policy, 2000 in February 2000, 
which provides a holistic approach to the programme. It enumerates various 
Strategies and Action Plan to achieve i mmediate, medium and long-term objectives. 
The Policy 
28 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
lists national socio-demographic goals for 2010 leading to population stabilization by 
2045.

THE MINISTER OF THE STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI):  (a) and (b) India ratified the 
Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer on June 19, 1991 and the 
Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer on September 17, 
1992. The Ozone Depleting Substances (Reg ulation and Control) Rules, 2000 have 
been notified in the Gazette of India on 19t h July, 2000. Important provisions of these 
Rules are given as under: 
(i) The Rules prohibit the use of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) in manufacturing 
various products beyond 1.1.2003 except for use in metered dose inhaler and 
other medical uses. Simila rly use of balloons are prohibited after 1.1.2001 
except for essential use. Other Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS) such as 
carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform  and CFC (in metere d dose inhalers) 
can be used for manufacture of products upto 1.1.2010. Further, the use of 
methyl bromide has been allowe d upto 1.1,2015. Since hydrochloro-
florocarbons (HCFCs) are used as inte rim substitute to re place CFCs these 
are allowed to be used upto 1.1.2040. 
(ii) It regulates production of Ozone Depleting Substances. They are to be phased 
out by 2010. 
(iii) The Rules have provisions for compulsory registration of ODS producers, 
manufacturers of ODS based products, importers, exporters stockist and 
sellers, and the same provision is appl icable to manufacturers, importers and 
exporters of compressors. 
(iv) The Rules provide for maintaining records and filing of periodic reports for 
monitoring production and use of ODS. 
(v) It also mandates that enterprises ho w have received financial assistance from 
Multilateral Fund have to register the da te of completion of their project and 
to declare that the equipment used for ODS has been destroyed. 
(vi) It prohibits creation of new capacity or expansion of capacity of manufacturing 
facilities of ODS and ODS based equipment.

(ix) Authority has been specified to issue licence for all imports and exports of 
ODS and products containing ODS.

approved by the Executive Committee of the Montreal Protocol in November, 1999.

1487. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the national programmes for ensuring quality education through improvement 
of teaching methods, teachers training and improvement of curriculum; 
(b) the State-wise target se t and status of allocate d amount sanctioned on each 
programme; and

Centrally sponsored scheme of Restruct uring and Reorganisation of Teachers 
Education (CTE) and sanctiona l status of each, including the proposal of Lakhimpur

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOU RCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) A Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Restructuring and 
Reorganisation of Teacher Education was started in 1987-88 to create an academic and 
technical resource base for orientation training and continuous upgradation of 
knowledge, competence and pedagogical skills of school teachers. The scheme 
envisages setting up of District  Institutes of Education & Training (DIETs), Colleges 
of Teacher Education (CTEs) and Institutes of Advanced Studies in Education 
(IASEs) to provide resource support to elementary, secondary and adult education. No 
State-wise targets are set. However, 50 DIETs, 100 CTEs and 40 IASEs are proposed

34 IASEs have been sanctioned. List of sanctioned projects, State and UT—wise, and 
amount allocated during the last three years is given in Statement-I. 
National Council for Education Research & Training (NCERT) organises inservice 
programmes for the faculty of DIETs, C TEs, IASEs  and  State Councils of 
Educational  Research  & Training

of teaching methods and curriculum. NCERT has also been organizing Special 
Orientation Programme for Primary School Teachers (SOPT) of the country to

in equipment and apparatus provided in the Operation Blackboard Scheme. Till now 
about 14,23,229 teachers have been trained in this programme. 
University Grants Commission (UGC) also strives to maintain high standards of 
teaching in universities and colleges through various programmes/schemes such as 
Academic Staff Colleges (ASCs), refresher courses conducted by select 
universities/special institutions, panels of experts in various subjects, curriculum 
development centres, Special Assistance Programmes for improvement of teaching 
and research, etc. Grants of Rs. 1485.53 lakhs under the programme of Academic Staff

professional qualification and competence. Details of Budget Allocation/Expenditure

THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS, SPORTS AND MINES (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Conventionally a Study Group

major minerals which comprises representati ves of State Governments, the Industry, 
the technical institutions and other concerned Ministries/ Departments. The Study 
Group makes recommendations about the rates of royalty after holding broad-based 
consultations which are considered by the Government and final revision of the rates 
of royalty is notified in the gazette. There is no proposal to set up any statutory body of 
experts for revision of royalty rates.

recommendations made on 14.9.97 suggested that the rate of royalty on lignite should 
be linked with that of coal. Based on th e recommendations of the Study Group, the 
Ministry of Coal is considering to enha nce the rate of royalty on lignite to a 
reasonable level. No periodici ty of revision of royalty ra tes on minerals including 
lignite has been laid down in law. The proviso to section 9(3) of the Mines and 
Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 stipulates that no enhancement of 
royalty rate on minerals can be done more than once during any period of three years.

(b) to (e) The Government allows foreign equity holding upto 100%, on the 
automatic route for all minerals (except diamonds and precious stones). This covers 
exploration, mining, mineral processing and metallurgy. In  the case of diamonds and 
precious stones, foreign equity upto 74% is allowed on the automatic route for both 
exploration and mining operations. For proposals seeking higher than 74% foreign 
equity, the cases go to the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) for 
approval. The Mines & Minerals [Development & Regulation] Act, 1957 has also 
been suitably amended and further powers have been delegated to the State 
Governments. These recent changes in the Act are expected to streamline the 
procedure for obtaining mineral concessions from the State Governments. They also 
provide adequate security of tenure to the investors. It is expected that these policy 
changes will lead to a faster growth and development of the Indian mineral sector, and 
also application of world class mining technology. 
The FIPB, in consultation with the Minist ry of Mines, has so far approved 65 
proposals of Foreign Direct Investment in the mining sector. The likely investment in 
these cases will be about Rs. 3650 crores . Most of these proposals speak only about 
their investment plans and do not specify the area where they would like to operate. It 
is not mandatory for an applicant company to specify the area-State where they would 
like to operate. The approval granted by FIPB is only for foreign equity participation 
in a Company incorporated in India. After obtaining FIPB approval these companies 
are required to apply to the concerned State Government, which are the owners of 
minerals in their respective territorial ju risdictions, for mineral concessions. Before 
granting the mineral concessions, State G overnments need the prior approval of the 
Central Government only in respect of minerals in the First Schedule of the Mines & 
Minerals [Development & Regulation] Act, 1957. The Central Government does not 
keep data of mineral concessions granted by State Governments.

The Ministry of Home Affairs had conve ned a meeting on 8-4-1996, to review the

Railway Police Chiefs in September, 1996 to  discuss the strategy to check crime on 
railways. Further a joint 
meeting was held in August, 1998 attended by the then Minister for Railways (MR.). 
The M.R. also convened a meeting of Chie f Secretaries and Directors General/Police 
of all State Governments and RPF officials in January, 2000.

DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) The universally accepted index of train accidents 
is number of train accidents per million kilometres. This index which stood at 5.5. in 
1960-61 has come down to 0.58 consequential train accidents per million train 
kilometres during the years 1997-98 and 1998-99. On Indian Railways, 
approximately 65 to 70% accidents are due to Railway staff failure. Railways

Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000) 
Some of the important steps being taken to prevent accidents are listed below: 
(i) The work of track circuiting has been accelerated on the trunk routes and 
other important main lines. 
(ii) Modification of the signalling circ uitry is being carried out to minimise 
chances of human error in causing accidents. 
(iii) Walkie-Talkie sets have been supplied to Drivers and Guards of all trains. 
(iv) There has been progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and ballast 
cleaning machines for track maintenance. 
(v) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics 
of the track, sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and 
portable accelerometers are being progressively used. 
(vi) For detecting rail fractures and we ld failures, 96 more double rail Ultra 
Sonic Flaw Detectors are being procured. 
(vii) Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been modernised and 
upgraded at many depots. 
(viii) To prevent cases of cold breakage of exles, Routine Over Hauling Depots 
have been equipped with ultrasonic testing equipment for detection of 
flaws in the exles. 
(ix) Whistle boards/speed breakers and road signs have been provided  at  
unmanned  level crossing and visibility  for 
drivers has been improved. 
(x) Periodic Safety Audit of different divisions by interdisciplinary teams 
from zonal headquarters has been introduced. 
(xi) Training facilities for drivers, guards and staff connected with train 
operation have been modernised inlcuding use of Simulators for training 
of drivers. 
(xii) Refresher courses are regularly organised at specified intervals.

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA

monitored and those found deficient are sent for attending crash courses.

among the staff.

Floods In Arunachal Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN (Karnataka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is reported 
that, last month, a dam in Tibet has breached, causing floods in Arunachal 
Pradesh, which claimed 30 lives. More than 100 tribals are missing, according 
to the official sources from the Arunachal Pradesh Government. The Tsango 
River, which originates in China flows into India and is called 'Siang' in 
Arunachal Pradesh, and 'Brahmaputra' in  Assam. More than 50,000 people in 
five districts of Arunachal Pradesh have been rendered homeless by the 
floods, while several parts of the State were cut off from the rest of the 
country. More than 20 big bridges, a lifeline for the people, have been washed 
away by strong currents. Even today, most of the villagers are taking shelter in 
temporary camps and huts. The loss is esti mated at 100 crores of rupees, It 
will take years for the areas, hit by the floods, to regain the original status. 
Arunachal Pradesh is a small State and a sensitive border St ate, it has no 
resources to meet such an unprecedented situation. It is obligatory on the 
part of the Central Government to rush aid to Arunachal Pradesh and sanction 
urgent funds for rehabilitat ion. The Central Government should not follow its 
usual time-consuming procedure to give aid. Instead, the Central Government 
should rush aid immediately. I dem and a statement from  the Government 
stating as to what action has been taken and how much relief has been given 
so far.

Distress Sale Of Paddy In Orissa 
DR. M, N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, this special mention is regarding the distress 
sale of paddy in Orissa. The super cyclone of October, 1999 rendered more 
than a million people homeless, destroye d lakhs of cattle .and inundated 
agricultural lands.with saline water. Ye t, the hapless farmers, faced with stark 
starvation, worked hard to raise high-yield crops like taichung and irate and 
did succeed. They purchased bullocks and fertilizers and hired labourers at a 
high wage. For such an investment they borrowed heavy   amounts of money.   
The investment resulted in excellent harvest.

But the poor and marginal farmers are now forced to go in for distress sale of 
paddy to pay back the loans. The cost of  cultivation per acre, on an average, 
comes to Rs.6,000 to Rs.6,500 due to rise in the prices of diesel, kerosene, 
fertilizers and pesticides. Yield per acre roughly comes to 15 quintals. The 
present rate of distress sale price per quintal being Rs.350 to Rs.370 only, the 
peasants suffer a loss of Rs. 1.250 per acre for cultivating the land, The 
Government does not purchase paddy at  the • support price of Rs,490 for 
common paddy and Rs.520 for fine paddy for lack of storage system. The 
season for monsoon cultivation having approached, peasants have no 
economic means to cultivate their fields. If the crop is not raised and harvest 
does not yield usual quantit y of paddy, the future of the peasantry will turn 
bleak. I request the Government to take timely steps.  Otherwise, Orissa will 
face a famine-like situation. 
Leasing of Airports and implementation of Airports Authority 
Of India Act. 1994. 
SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu):   Sir, the subject of my special 
mention is leasing of airports and impl ementation of the Airports Authority of 
India Act, 1994. 
Sir, the recent decision of the Cabine t Committee to go in for a long-term 
lease of five airports to the private sector is causing concern because it will 
lead to a huge loss to the exchequer and the security of our nation will be at 
stake. This move will result in the revenue loss of Rs.130 crores per year. 
Thirteen airports have a combined profit of Rs.400 crores and 107 airports 
suffer a loss of Rs.83 crores. The Airports Authority of India is. the only 
organisation making profit in the civil aviation industry. To overcome this loss of 
Rs.83 crores, Alports Authority of India Act, 1994 was passed to merge 
international and national divisions and to  bring it under one authority, that is, 
AAI, for the development of all airports. 
The merger of both the divisions has not yet been implemented. Instead, 
the Government is going opposite by clearing the decks in favour of long-term 
lease to enable the Indian airports to attain global standards. World-class 
facilities should not be compromised at the cost of national security. 
Furthermore, the wage revision for the employees in the officers cadre has 
been implemented with retrospective effect, while the Group C and D 
employees are staging demonstrations and dharnas for its implementation In 
the negotiations between the managemen t and the workers, the management 
has agreed to pay an advance amount to Group

National Agricultural Insurance Scheme 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA RADDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh has started implementing the National 
Agricultural insurance Scheme from Kharif 2000 onwards. As per the 
guidelines of the Scheme, the cut-off date for payment of premium and 
enrolment of non-loanee farmers is gi ven as one month after sowing/planting 
or 31st July, whichever is earlier. This stipulation is causing inconvenience to 
the non-loanee farmers as most of the rainfed crops in Andhra Pradesh will be 
continued to be sown even beyond the months of July and August. After 
thorough discussion in the SLCC meeting and considering the time of sowing 
of different crops in different districts,  the cut-off dates for loanee farmers are 
fixed ranging from the end of September to end of December. In this regard, f 
submit that when the cut-off dates be yond 31st July are fixed for loanee 
farmers, it would be appropriate to adopt the same method for the non-loanee 
farmers as well so that many non-loan ee farmers can become stakeholders in 
the new Scheme. Hence, I request the Mini stry of Agriculture to consider the 
special circumstances prevailing in Andhra Pradesh and permission may be 
accorded to keep the cut-off dates for non-loanee farmers on par with the 
loanee farmers so that uniformity in cut-off dates for different crops grown in 
the State can be maintained, which, I am sure, would attract more non-loanee 
farmers under the scheme. Thank you.

STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER 
Recent massacre in various places in Jammu and Kashmir 
THE PRIME MINISTER (SHRI ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE): Mr. Chairman. Sir, I 
visited Pahalgam and Srinagar on Thursday (3.8.2000) to study the situation arising 
out of recent massacre in various places in Jammu and Kashmir and of pilgrims at 
Pahalgam. I am thankful to Shrimati S onia Gandhi, Shri Somnath Chatterjee, 
Shri Mulayam Singh Yadav, Shri Yerrannaldu and Shri Ghulam Nabi Azad for 
agreeing to pin me at such a short notice. My colleagues, Shri George Fernandes, 
Kumari Mamata Banerjee and Shri Chaman Lat Gupta also joined me along with the 
Chief of Army Staff. From Srinagar, the Governor and the Chief Minister of Jammu 
and Kashmir accompanied us. 
Our visit was also intended to assure the people of the State that the entire 
nation stood by them at this hour and to  share their grief over the inhuman 
behaviour of the terrorists against innocent people belonging to the State as well as 
many from other parts of the country on pilgrimage to Amarnath. 
The briefing which we were given by the Chief of the Unified Command and 
security forces, made ft dear that perpetrators of these heinous crimes were 
foreigners. Arms and ammunitions recovered from them clearly establish their links 
with Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Toiba. 
Delegations of local population as well as pilgrims met me and spoke to me 
about the difficulties they were facing in the wake of the killings. 
The House, I am sure, is one with me in assuring the people of Jammu and 
Kashmir and the nation that we will not yield before terrorism. I may add that while 
the fight against terrorism will be continued, India will not give up efforts for 
restoration of peace in Jammu and Kashmir. 
I made it dear at Srinagar that the dialogue with Hizbul Mujahideen Is a part of 
this effort. Other groups who have chosen the path of violence should also 
realise that the people of Jammu and Kashmir want peace in the State. It is futite 
for them to continue on the path of violence. They

SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Sir. we welcome the process of

eventuaUy, the process of dialogue would persuade the other misguided 
sections to join the dialogue and find a peaceful solution to this problem. Sir, we all 
know that there are certain elements, both inside the country and outside the country, 
who want to scuttle this process, who want to divide India. The present experience, 
once more, brings to our notice that much more is required there - much more 
vkjHance '» required, much more security measures are required. Would the

SHRI P.N. SIVA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, at the ou tset, I congratulate the Prime

to congratulate the leaders of the other parties who accompanied him and

this issue is concerned, it has been es tablished that despite the political 
differences, we are all united. I, belonging to a party which condemns violence 
and terrorism in any manner from any quarter of this country, would like to

The clarification that we would like to ha ve from the Prime Minister is this. In

in the Army are aware that they have to attack and they will be attacked, but 
not the innocent people who fall victims to  these terrorists. Again, I appreciate

continue. India will not give up its effo rts for restoration of peace in Jammu 
and Kashmir. Sir, I support the three-phased approach which has been 
planned by this Government, namely, to have a dialogue with the people who 
are against this, that is, with those milit ants who are established there, and to 
fight terrorism, along with improving t he economic condition of the people of 
Jammu and Kashmir, which alone will impr ove the situation. My contention is 
that Mahatma Gandhiji has left behind many things to be followed by us. One 
of those things is to resist. We will not yield to terrorism. We  will not yield to 
violence. And we will not yield to this sort of threat from any quarter. So, the 
fight against terrorism will continue. Let us put an end to terrorism with all the 
might, and our cooperation is always with you. Thank you,

.the appeal made by the Prime Minister that the other militant

any compensation to these

Border, the Indo-Bhutan Border; and to st art fruitful talks with the Bhutan, 
Pakistan and Bangladesh Governments to see that they do not give shelter to 
these militant outfits. 
It is found that Bhutan and Pakistan are very much affectionate and 
sympathetic to the militant outfits, and the militants are taking shelter and 
having training in the use of arms there. 
Sir, I am expressing my sincere sympathy to the affected people, their 
211 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
families and the security personnel and pray for eternal peace for the departed 
souls. 
Sir, I further request the hon. Prime Mini ster to look into the matter, in the 
greater interest of the people of our country. 
Thank you. Sir. 
SHRI R.S. GAVAI (Maharashtra): Mr.  Chairman, Sir. at the outset, I 
welcome the visit of the hon. Prime Minister to Pahalgam, which was very 
timely, and also the assurance given by hi m to the people of the State that the 
entire nation stood by them and shared th eir grief over the inhuman behaviour 
of the terrorists. I also welcome his stat ement that the dialogue with the Hizbul 
Mujahideen is part of his effort. We believe in dialogues and negotiations. 
At the same time, I want to seek some clarifications from the Prime 
Minister. Earlier, it was made amply clear by the Government that the 
negotiations with the Hizbul would be with in the framework of the Constitution 
and not beyond the purview of the Constitution. Are the Prime Minister and the 
Government of India adopting this stand now also? 
K has appeared in a section of the Press that Mujibur Rehman has some 
pre-conditions. He has said that he woul d appreciate a- direct or indirect 
intervention. That is one of the conditi ons. So, in the greater interest of our 
integrity and having regard and respect to the Indian Constitution, I want to 
seek a clarification from the Prime Minister on these two conditions. Earlier, the 
statement made by the Union Government  was that it would stick to the 
purview of the Constitution and that no mediation by Pakistan would be 
permitted. I hope the Government of Indi a, particularly the Prime Minister and 
the Home Minister, will stick to the stand. 
Thank you very much. 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU (Karnataka); Mr. Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
component the Prime Minister as well as  the various leaders of the Opposition 
for having taken an immediate initiative, having gone over there and having 
expressed their concern and solidarity with the people there. This is a 
challenge before the nation, and the nation stands united to fight this 
challenge. 
The second point I want to make is th at the country should not be seen in 
this array, as if we are asking for each other's help. We should stand united 
and expose the evil designs of the enemies who want to create problems. 
212 

|4 August. 2000) RAJYA SABHA 
Third. It Is a continuous battle. It is a proxy war going on for the last 
20 years. According to the Information I have, our country has lost 23,000 
persons in Kashmir alone in these years, It to not a normal number. We 
really feel sorry for what has happened all these years. 
Fourth. ex-Prime Ministers of this country and ex-Chief Ministers have 
been killed. .These militants, terrorists, these inhuman people, are choosing 
their targets. Similarly, they have targeted the Amarnath Yatris. It is highly 
condemnable, and the entire nation should condemn this. 
The Prime Minister has said that the fight against terrorism would 
continue and that we would not depart from the path, the peace prorata, 
that we have chosen. At the same time, a question that is agitating the 
minds of the people of the entire country--we are receiving calls from 
different parts of the country-is: what about the other people who have not 
given up their arms? 
They are continuing with their activities. They may Indulge in some 
more activities also. As has been pointed out by one hon. Member 
yesterday, they do not have any Identity, any badge that they belong to the 
Hizbul Mujahideen or Lashkar-e-Totoe or Harkat-ut-Anaar. No such easy 
identification Is available for these people in that area. That being the case, 
I do not want the Prime Minister to tell this House in what way he to going 
to proceed, but the point is that the people want that immediate action 
should be taken against these people who are indulging in these activities. 
Mobilise all the forces that is required and crush these people mercilessly, 
because the entire nation wants peace. These people, and a few of them 
who are aided from outside, are indulging in these heinous crimes. That 
being the case, the people want the Government to act. As the Prime 
Minister has said, nobody disputes that there are some lepsos somewhere. 
Who is responsible for that? If there to some security lapse, security forces 
alone will be able to Identify those lapses and rectify them, take note of 
what exactly had happened and then take remedial measures. I, for one, 
am not in agreement with the demand for a judicial inquiry because nothing 
will be proved, because It is a security matter. An officer in charge of the 
security forces should be asked to conduct the Inquiry and take remedial 
steps. But going back to the original point, our Immediate concern is to 
fight the enemy and nobody should think that we are divided amongst 
ourselves. Will asking for the head of somebody or some Minister solve the 
matter? As i told you, the Prime Minister of this country was shot dead in 
her own house,   it is a sad thing that we lost a great leader.   The same 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
thing happened in the case of one of our former Prime Ministers. The same 
thing happened with one Chief Minister of Punjab. Instead of trying to score 
some points, I appeal to one and all with all humility with a deep sense of 
concern at my heart as this is a national challenge, let us fight this together 
unitedly.

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY (Andhra Pradesh) : Sir, I move 
the following Resolution: - 
"Having regard to the fact that- 
(i) the population of our count ry has reached an alarming 
number crossing one billion mark in May, 2000; 
(ii) the increasing population is the root cause of poverty, 
 unemployment, corruption, crime and social unrest;  
(iii) due to increased population, the results of development 
have not reached the common people; and 
(iv) all the measures taken to check the population during the  
last 50 years have not yielded the desired results, 
this House urges upon the Government to take immediate steps such 
as giving incentives to the people having small family; making small 
family norm compulsory for the people's representatives and 
employees; evolving a consensus with political parties and religious 
groups on making small family norms compulsory for all and starting 
a mass movement involving various government agencies and 
NGO's to spread the messa ge about the necessity of small family to 
the masses." 
India is the first country in the world to take up the population control 
programme, this programme was started in 1952, and since our country was 
the first country to start this progra mme, it should have remained as an ideal 
country in regard to population control and family welfare programmes. But our 
country has miserably failed in achieving the targeted results and we have not 
been able to stop the population growth. For implementing the family welfare 
and family planning programmes, the kind  of dedication and devotion that is 
required by the implementing agencies is lacking. Our officers and leaders 
have not been able to give a proper directio n to this. As a result of all this, our 
country today has remained as the second largest populated country in the 
world. The family planning programmes have been full of various loopholes 
and shortcomings due to which the people have not been enlightened about 
the family planning programmes. India, today, has got 100 crore people; that 
means one billion people. Mr. Vice-Chairman,  Sir, in the next 50 years, we will 
go ahead of China and will become the largest populated country in the world. 
Whatever measures we may take, this situation cannot be stopped under any 
circumstances.. Do we feel happy about having a one billion population?  I am 
sure, doubt we are not. 
226 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA  
Every year, 17 million people are being added to the population of the 
country. 
By this, the demand on our resources, housing, clothing, health and education 
facilities is increasing day by day and these resources are becoming scarce. Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, due to this, whatever achievements we are making in the 
economic, educational and technological fields are being sidetracked and we are not 
able to make better use of the achievements we are making in all the other fields. 
We have to feel very sad about this kind of situation prevailing in the country. It 
was stated that in the First Five Year Plan that for achieving economic growth, we 
have to check the growth of population. In the Second Five Year Plan, it was felt 
that the growth of population was much more than the expected level and it was likely 
to continue for a longer period. Therefore, in the succeeding Five-Year Plans, the 
small family norm has been considered as the foundation for development. In 
spite of eight Five-Year Plans and five decades of planning, we have not been 
able to reduce the growth of population. The main reason for this is the lower 
allocation of funds for the family planning programmes. According to the report of 
the World Bank given in 1993, among the developing countries, India is one of the 
countries spending the lowest amount on family planning programmes. Even the 
allocated amount is not being spent adequately and properly. Therefore, the 
Government has to seriously consider increasing the allocation for family welfare 
programmes. Government should also plug the loopholes 'to ensure proper and 
adequate utilisation of the funds granted. Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, Government has 
totally failed in bringing awareness among the people and enlightening them about 
the necessity of. the family welfare programmes. As everyone is aware, ours is a 
traditional and custom-oriented.,, society where old customs are given more 
prominence and importance. Among most of the families, even today, there is a 
strong desire for at least one son; if not two. We have not been able to change 
this custom. Due to this, the fertility rate is still hovering around 3.5 per cent. It is 
unfortunate that after 50 years of our incessant effort, we have not been able to 
reduce the fertility rate, whereas many other developing nations have taken around 
15 years only for bringing about this much change. In 1983, the National Health 
Policy was prepared. According to the National Health Policy  the fertility rate in our 
country was to come down to 2.1 percent by the year 2000. But in achieving this, 
our Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and all the programmes that have been 
adopted have totally failed.   I am constrained to note that according to the Registrar 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
General of India, we will be able to achi eve this fertility rate only in 2006. But 
many experts feel that this may not be possible even by then. We have not 
even reached the most impor tant and most difficult ob jective that is, adoption 
of the one child norm by the people. For ta king up that concept, first of all, we 
have to eradicate the custom and the feeling among the people that they 
should have minimum of two sons. Thereafter, we have also to eradicate and 
remove the feeling among the people of having at least one son. After 
crossing these two steps, we will be able to take the small family norm to the 
people and convince them about it. I hav e come to know that recently the 
National Population Commission has also recommended the introduction of 
the two-child norm. 
I strongly urge upon the Government to seriously consider the 
implementation of the 'small family' norm and even the 'one child' norm. 
According to the famous scientist, Dr. Swaminathan, adopting a holistic 
approach is the only way to stop the population growth. I also agree with his 
view. According to him, 'It should be the right of every child to have all the 
basic necessities, to have a healthy lif e, education and nutritious food.' These 
are the basic requirements that are needed. 
Because of the incentives that hav e been incorporated in our family 
planning programmes, we have not been able to bring awareness among the 
people. Had we considered -- instead of incentives - providing literacy, 
education, economic safety, social empowerment, etc., we could have 
achieved the desired growth in the family planning programmes. Development 
should be linked with reproductive health because population, poverty, 
production and consumption are all inter-linked. Therefore, we have to achieve 
a lot in the economic and educational se ctors so that the results of that 
achievement will have this impact on the implementation of family welfare 
programmes. We are backward even in  the health sector. Even though our 
country has a very wide and large health network system, sufficient medical 
facilities are not available to the people, and majority of the population do not 
get even the minimum medical facilities. According to the estimates of the 
World Health Organisation, five beds have to be there for every one thousand 
population. But, in our country, the si tuation is the other way round. It is 
between 2 and 2.06 beds in the cities, and in the villages, It is much lower. The 
doctor ratio is also very bad in our country. According to the  statements made 
here, in this House, ther e is one doctor for nearly 30,000 people. There is one 
doctor for every 15,000 - 20,000 people In States Iike Andhra Pradesh, 
Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh; 
228 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
same is the case with beds. In fact, majority of the villages in our country do 
not have any medical facilities. Simi larly, the ratio of doctors, nurses and 
hospitals vis-a-vis population is very le ss. By this, we can understand that the 
people in our country do not have the mi nimum health facilities. I, therefore, 
say that when we achieve full coverage of health facilities to all the people and 
provide economic security to the people, we will be able to go a step forward 
in the direction of reducing the population growth. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, we are also  neglecting our Indian Systems of 
Medicine such as Ayurveda, Homeo, Sidha, Unani, Naturopathy, etc., which 
were very popular in the olden days. T hese are also result-oriented systems. I 
do not know why our country is neglect ing these systems. We can have good 
results if we adopt these systems, with Jess budget. This aspect has to be 
gone into. I request that the Government should think about these systems. 
Sir, literacy is the main  measuring instrument for population growth. No 
other aspect can reduce the population as much as literacy. The main reason 
for not achieving the desired results in the family welfare programmes is, 
illiteracy and inability to bring awarenes s among the people. Illiteracy, among 
women, is the main problem. Though it is the women who should be the 
forerunners in implementing the family planning programmes, majority of the 
women are illiterate. According to one survey, one woman out of four does not 
have awareness about the birth control methods. Women in the age group of 
13-30 are not able to keep a gap between the children under the modem 
temporary contraception methods. In our country, 65 per cent of the girls get 
married between the age of 13 and 18, All these things are happening due to 
illiteracy; If .there were literacy and education among women, they would have 
had awareness which would have brought wonders in the implementation of 
this programme. The main example of this is Kerala, Since Kerala has 
achieved total literacy, 80 per cent of the girls marry only between the age 
group of 25 and 30. In this State, the birth rate is 16.7 per cent, whereas the 
target set for the country is 20 per cent. But in Uttar Pradesh, the birth rate is 
36.8 per cent, in Bihar it is 36.2 per cent. By this, we can understand the 
importance of education in achieving the desired results in the family welfare 
programme. 
Recently, our Government has announced the National Population 
Policy. I am constrained to note that even though our country was the first 
country to start a country-wide family planning programme, we have taken 50 
years to prepare such a policy document.  However, I am still glad that, 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
at least now, the policy has been fina lised. This policy contains many 
programmes. Some of the programmes worth-mentioning are: reducing the 
maternal mortality rate, the infant mortality rate, and keeping the contraceptive 
services within the reach of the people, Many incentives have been 
incorporated in this. Some of them are:  giving rewards to Panchayats and Zila 
Parishads, continuing Balika Samridhi Yojna, Maternity Welfare Scheme, 
Health Insurance Scheme, etc. However, there are some drawbacks in this 
also. Women have not been given the desired role and importance, Women's 
social and economic empowerment is very essential for the family welfare 
programme. But in the National Population Policy, only a passing reference 
has been made. I, therefore, request the Government to consider re-
examining the policy and give sufficient orientation to women. Giving rewards 
acts as a major curse for women. It is_ mainly because Panchayats and Zila 
Parishads make use of the poor people, particularly women, for reaching the 
targets and getting rewards. This is not my view; this is the apprehension 
expressed by many experts. Many more apprehensions have been expressed 
on the policy. Therefore, Governm ent should examine the apprehensions 
expressed by the experts on the Nati onal Population Policy. Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, Another most distressin g fact is that the BIMARU States - 
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh -- contribute the 
maximum to the population growth of t he country. However, their contribution 
towards the effort at reducing the popula tion growth is negligible. These four 
States account 60 per cent of the populati on growth of the country; while their 
population is only 40 per cent of the total population of the country. By this, we 
can understand to what extent the family planning programmes are neglected 
in these four States. Ther efore, a special programme with an intensified effort 
is required in these four States so t hat the country can think of reducing the 
population growth. The role of non-governmental organizations in 
implementing the family planning programmes and bringing awareness among 
the people, is significant. In fact, these organizations can play a better role 
than the Government in educating the pe ople on this. I, therefore, request the 
Government to give sufficient role to NGOs. 
Now, I come to the 79th Constitution {Amendment) Bill. This BUI, I think, 
was introduced in the Rajya Sabha in 1992. This Bill provides for promotion of 
the small family norm and making efforts to reduce population growth. But the 
important aspect of the B ill is that those who have more than two children will 
not be eligible to be elected as Members of Parliament and State Legislatures.   
This is a very important aspect, and if 
230 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
this can be implemented, the elected representatives can become the role 
model for the people. The Stand ing Committee on Human Resource 
Development has considered this Bill and su bmitted its report in 1995. In this 
report, the Committee has made many recommendations. It was 
recommended that by taking the small family norm as the main aspect, the 
population growth should be stabilised at the replacement level and this should 
be the main target of the country. The Committee, while fully supporting the 
Bill, felt that every political party should keep the small family norm in the Code 
of Conduct for Members. The Co mmittee has also recommended that 
incentives and disincentives should be given for the people of all sectors, 
mainly Government employees, teachers , professionals, private sector, etc. 
But the main recommendation of the Commi ttee in regard to the eligibility 
criteria, on the basis of small family no rm, for being elected to Parliament and 
State Legislatures, is that the Go vernment should have wide-ranging 
consultations with all political parties and leaders and arrive at a consensus, 
and the Bill should be passed. Unfortunately,  this Bill has not seen the light of 
the day. I do not know to what extent the Government had consultations to 
arrive at a consensus. I am constrained to say that our Government has not 
given sufficient importance to such an important piece of Legislation. If this Bill 
is passed, we, the Members of Parliame nt and State Legislatures, can be the 
role model for the entire population of the country. 
The question was proposed.

DR. A.R, KIDWAI (Delhi): Mr. Vice-Chairman, I am very happy that this important 
subject has come up for discussion, lixfia has a large population. In spite of having a 
large number of natural resources and self-sufficiency in food, it cannot develop and 
utilise them to bring prosperity to the common people because it is unable to control 
its population. With a population of one billion, the matter has become very urgent 
and important. Therefore, the Resolution should be given serious consideration. 
The policy adopted for the year 2000 is to get the support of non-government 
organisations, corporate sector and industry to promote it as a national campaign, 
this is an important subject, and it cannot  be delayed any further. In order to 
tackle the problem, it has to be dealt with on a national scale, as a national 
population movement. 
234 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
The policy paper that has been pre pared is quite comprehensive and 
good, But there are some deficiencies t hat have to be looked into. In India, 
now that we have adopted the Panchay at system, if we strengthen the 
Panchayats, charge them with this task, provide them the facilities to 
implement this programme and also educate people about this important 
subject of population control, I think,  it will provide the most effective 
mechanism to promote the population control policies. 
But the other aspect that has been negl ected is the utilisation of the 
maternity and child welfare services. It is  the most effective method that goes 
directly to the people in the reproductive age. If the family welfare 
programmes are linked with the maternity and child welfare services and if the 
methods are advised as part of the chil d welfare and maternity services, then, 
it will be the most effective and most acceptable method. 
in Bihar, the British Governors had esta blished 29 hospitals, specifically 
for maternity and child welfare services. They are defunct and not in use. But 
three of these hospitals in Patna were activated with the help of the 
Department of Welfare of the Governm ent of India, and. today, they are 
producing the best results. Poor people,  those who cannot afford, go to these 
places. They are the right places wher e these problems can be tackled. Due 
to the help available from the Welfare Department in reactivating the 
maternity and child welfare programme, these three hospitals have become- 
centres of activity. Even the best gynaecologists in the city gave their free 
time, and it attracted a lot of people. They have started producing results now. 
Why can the remaining 26 hospitals also not be reactivated? 
Really the best approach and the right approach to provide effective child 
welfare and maternity services is to provide them through the child welfare 
and maternity programmes in all hospitals, which should be strengthened. 
The effect of propaganda and incentives is doubtful. But every penny spent on 
strengthening the maternity and child we lfare services will not only provide 
good maternity and child welfare services but will also make it one of the most 
effective services to serve the community and to control the population. 
We should not hesitate to introduce cour ses on this subject as part of the 
school education system or as extra courses so that every young man and 
woman should know how it could be done. They should be properly educated 
as. part of education on health. 
235 

RAJYA SABHA 14 August, 2000] 
Earlier, a paper on health and hygiene was a compulsory paper in schools. It is 
no more so now. Such a compulsory paper is  all the more necessary now, because the 
people will not only be able to know about population control, family welfare, but will 
also be able to develop their health, their capacity to work and avoid diseases, by 
making up the deficiencies which they may have, by taking the required nutritional 
diet. Therefore, revival of such a compulso ry paper at the primary or secondary stage 
of education is all the more necessary. The family welfare programme is a serious 
programme, but it cannot be managed by flow of funds alone. It cannot be managed by 
propaganda or by giving incentives, which are generally misuse d. The programme 
should be developed on a concrete and solid basis so that the results are obvious and 
are beneficial to the people, I am sure, the Health Minister, who is aware of the 
intricacies of the programme, will re-orientate and integrate the family welfare 
schemes and bring the health services closer  to the people, ft is the only method to 
promote family welfare. Thank you.

SHRIMATI SHABANA AZM! (Nominated): Thank you, Sir, for giving me 
this opportunity to speak. I rise in su pport of the views expressed by Shrimati 
Sarla Maheshwari. It is also one of the rare instances when I support the views 
expressed by Shri Narendra Mohan. I share his disappointment, which he 
expressed in his opening remarks, that only a marginal number of people are 
present in the House when we are debating and discussing such an important 
issue. I wonder how this issue will get the consideration it deserves, if we have 
only a very few people present here. Sir,  as a member  of the  National  
Commission on Population and as 
242 

[4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the United Nations Ambassador on Population and Development, I want to 
make here a few submissions. India was one of the 180 nations who was' a 
signatory to the International Conference Oh Population and Development in 
1984 in Cairo. As a result of which in  October 1997, we came up with a very 
good, reproductive child health policy.  Unfortunately, however, that policy 
remained a closely guarded secret, I am  certain tnat if a survey were 
conducted in. Parliament, we would realise that most of the hon. Members of 
Parliament had no idea as to what the policy was. I fear, Sir, that the same 
situation might apply when it comes to the National Population Policy. After 
many deliberations and great debates and a lot of thought, we finally have a 
very good policy in place. I think the Government is serious about it. The 
Ministry is serious about it. It is very interesting to note that a couple of days 
ago, there was a question on population in Parliament, To my surprise, a very 
detailed answer was given by the Ministry which is the opposite of most of the 
answers given, I congratulate the Minist ry. I share the view that they are 
concerned about it. But. Sir, no policy can be effective If it remains as a good 
policy only on paper. We have to make sure that the mechanisms of 
implementation are put in place and that is the question that I need to put. First 
of all, this policy needs to be congrat ulated on the fact that it has done away 
with disincentives. It has, instead, fo cused on empowerment of women; 
improving the quality of care; bringing awareness on spacing of children; 
involving male participation and many other things. Today, when we are saying 
that this Population Policy will not becom e a reality in our country until and 
unless we make it a people's campaign, it  is extremely important that we, as 
Members of Parliament, first internalise what this policy is about. I think we 
have not internalised it. That is expressed in the fact that we still use the word 
'control' when we are talking about popul ation stabilisation, we are still talking 
about disincentives. Time and again, the question of disincentives comes up. 
What I would like to ask the hon. Minist er is this. What Is the Government's 
view when States take up a position on disincentives which is different from 
that expressed in the National Populati on Policy. It is very unfortunate that 
States like Madhya Pradesh already hav e legislations which say that people 
will be barred from standing in elections  at the Panchayat level if they have 
more than two children after January 2001. Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan 
have already endorsed it. I think this is a very sad state of affairs. Firstly, It is in 
conflict with the fresh National Population Policy. Secondly, I think such a 
measure violates the Constitution and is against the rights of women.  It is 
evident that in our society women do not 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
decide the number of children they are going to have. They have absolutely no 
say in this matter. By insisting on a legislation like that, you are further denying 
women an opportunity to get into politics. On the one hand, we are .talking 
about empowerment of women and on th e other hand, we are putting into 
place a legislation which is going to further disallow women from participating 
in the political process. So this is a very, very disturbing element that has been 
expressed by certain States. I wish to know as to what the Centre is going to 
do since this is in conflict with the policy that the Centre has announced. 
When it comes to the policy, as expres sed on paper, it is good; it stresses 
on quality of service, safe motherho od, controlling infant mortality and 
maternal mortality, male participation, creating awareness on the advantage of 
spacing children, having a small family  and so on. But how is it going to 
happen? At what level is it going to hap pen? At the micro level, what do we 
intend to do about it? Much has been said about using the Panchayats and 
much has been said as to how the Panchayats and Zilla Parishads will be 
involved; how the ANMs will be involved; how the primary health centres will 
be involved, The fact was that when independent surveys were conducted, it 
had been found different. The ANMs simply do not have the means of 
reaching the far-flung areas because they have no means of transport. Very 
often, they don't have the basic essentia l drugs that are required. On the other 
hand, the recipients say that they cannot use the primary sub-centres because 
they don't even know when they are open; they open them at any time. So, at 
the micro level, there are all these considerations. T here is also a distrust 
among the people. I was recently in a village where I asked an ANM; "What 
has been her experience?" She said, "One of the most successful 
programmes has been the polio immunisation programme and even in that 
programme, there is such a distrust of  Government services that when two 
times the Government o fficers came fo rward with the programme, they 
welcomed it, but the third time there wa s this feeling of distrust,   anfa? * T?T

TOi <re> itof H<*§& 3>i crater t, it Is a crime shame that the number of 
women who die of pregnancy-related diseases, of pregnancy-related Issues. in 
one week in India is more than in all of Europe in a whole year. In actual ier/ns, 
the experts in the fields have said that 70 per cent of these deaths 
244 

(4 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA" 
are entirety preventable by taking very  small measures such as" giving them. 
tetanus shots, making sure that they get iron tablets for controlling their 
anemia, and giving them pre-natal and post-natal care. These are entirely 
preventable things. Now, unfortunately, in  our country, this is not an emotive 
issue; the death of mothers during pregn ancy is not an emotional issue. If this 
is not an emotional issue, then what else should become an emotional issue? 
Shall I take the same statistics and give  it to you in another way? The number 
of women who die in one year in India due to pregnancy-related issues would 
be the same if we had 300 airplane crashes  a year. Can you imagine if this is 
what we were to give in the newspap ers, then the entire Government would 
fall? So, when it comes to women and their health, nobody makes it an 
emotive issue. Unless it becomes an emotive issue, it will not become a 
people's campaign; it will not become internalised amongst us. That is why 
health and, particularly, women's health , has to be put on the agenda. Now, 
there are views expressed constantly that  we have to control the total fertility 
rate, that we have to somehow or the other bring down the total fertility rate. 
And often enough, China is given as an example. Firstly, we are a different 
Government from China and, of course, we cannot have that kind of controls 
that China has. And in spite of that, y ou have to understand that there is this 
feeling that if you can somehow bring down the total fertility rate, then, you are 
automatically going to reduce poverty. But then let us look at the figures; let us 
look at a country like Bangladesh which has reduced its. total fertility rate by 
half in the last 10 years, and yet it  continues to be amongst the poorest 
countries in the world. Unless China had not invested simultaneously in the 
social sector, invested in .education, invested in the health sector, it would not 
have had the kind of achievement that it has now. So we have to make a 
simultaneous investment in the social sect or. Sir, it is true that on 11th May, 
the population of India became 1 billio n which means that every sixth person 
in the world is an Indian 
This rings alarm bells in us. We look upon it like a time-bomb ticking away 
and, of course, the reaction is that so mehow or the other we have to control 
this. This is a dangerous view-point. What we are saying and what the 
National Policy on Population is saying is  that there has to be a multi-pronged 
approach towards- the population problem.  Disincentives and controls are not 
going to work. They haven't worked in any other country. We have the best 
examples in our own country within the States of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Goa. 
Let us took at those exampl es and follow those examples,   Let   us   not   
keep   talking   about   controls. or disincentives. 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2000] 
Let us also understand that there is an inbuilt momentum, at the moment. There, are 
240 million people in the age group of 10-24 and if they have even one child each, 
which they have the right to, we are still not going to be able to stabilise our 
population at the rate at which we want to. That is why it-is important that we have 
this multi-pronged attack on this issue, we understand it in all its complexity and, 
absolutely, do not allow talks on disincentives and, particularly, the view that people 
will be debarred from standing for elections if they have more than two children.
